results.summary: The design covers the full ML deployment lifecycle with versioned training, registry-based promotion, A/B inference, monitoring, and automated retraining, while keeping lineage and operational control explicit.

findings.title: Managed pipeline keeps training, deployment, and retraining tightly coordinated
findings.explanation: Step Functions coordinates versioned data preparation, training, evaluation, model registration, gated deployment, and retraining triggers. This gives the design a clear control plane for the full ML lifecycle rather than a loose collection of services.

findings.title: Lineage is preserved across data, training, registry, and monitoring artifacts
findings.explanation: The design carries dataset versions, code digests, run IDs, artifact digests, and registry source references through the pipeline, which is a strong basis for model lineage and experiment reproducibility.

results.summary: A coherent global CDN design using Route 53, CloudFront, S3, dynamic origin, Lambda@Edge, ACM, Shield, and CloudWatch to meet global delivery, low latency, customization, HTTPS, DDoS protection, invalidation, and monitoring needs.

findings.title: Edge customization is scoped to location-aware behavior
findings.explanation: Lambda@Edge is present specifically for request/response customization based on location, which matches the brief without overextending into unrelated shared-cache personalization.

findings.title: Global delivery path is clear and minimal
findings.explanation: The design uses Route 53 to resolve the hostname to CloudFront, then serves viewers directly from the CDN with separate static and dynamic origins. That is a coherent, low-latency global CDN topology.

findings.title: Monitoring covers the key CDN signals
findings.explanation: CloudFront metrics and Lambda@Edge telemetry are routed to CloudWatch, giving the design visibility into cache behavior, viewer latency, origin requests, and edge execution.

results.summary: The design covers configuration tracking, audit logging, threat detection, compliance evaluation, automated remediation, reporting, and centralized review with coherent AWS-native flows across accounts.

findings.title: Centralized compliance evidence and audit path is well decomposed
findings.explanation: The design separates configuration monitoring, threat detection, archival logging, remediation, reporting, and review into distinct services with clear data flows. That keeps the compliance/audit responsibilities understandable and traceable.

findings.title: Cross-account logging and compliance aggregation are explicitly represented
findings.explanation: AWS Organizations boundaries, organization trails, organization-level Config view, and centralized Security Hub aggregation together show the intended multi-account posture rather than single-account logging.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent AWS data lake with S3-based raw and curated zones, Glue cataloging and ETL, Athena SQL access, Lake Formation governance, QuickSight visualization, and CloudWatch operational visibility.

findings.title: Direct lake-query path is well aligned with the no-copy analytics requirement
findings.explanation: Athena reads curated S3 objects directly using Glue Catalog metadata, which matches the core 'query data without moving it' requirement and helps minimize data movement costs.

findings.title: Governance path covers both catalog and query-time authorization
findings.explanation: Lake Formation is connected to the catalog, ETL, and Athena, so the design shows governed metadata plus enforced access checks across ingestion and analytics flows.

findings.title: Operational visibility is integrated into both query and ETL paths
findings.explanation: CloudWatch receives Athena scan/queueing/denial signals and Glue job/schema health, giving the design observability over the main lake lifecycle without extra unused components.

results.summary: A coherent AWS leaderboard design with trusted score ingestion, ordered stream projection, Redis read acceleration, DynamoDB persistence, season rotation, and scoped friend/global ranking support.

findings.title: Server-authoritative score path reduces cheat surface
findings.explanation: Score updates are accepted only from trusted game servers and are revalidated for sequence, membership, season, and idempotency before publication, which fits the anti-cheat scope.

findings.title: Read-optimized projection supports instant ranking queries
findings.explanation: Using Redis sorted sets for top-K and rank lookups gives a clear low-latency read path without putting ranking work on the write path.

findings.title: Season rotation is handled without destructive rewrites
findings.explanation: The season coordinator updates the active namespace and persists the boundary, which is a clean mechanism for periodic leaderboard resets while preserving history.

results.summary: The architecture covers device enrollment, high-volume telemetry ingestion, real-time processing, anomaly detection, durable command delivery, visualization, lifecycle management, and five-year retention with coherent Azure component choices.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end device-to-command path
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates enrollment, telemetry ingestion, anomaly processing, and command dispatch, with acknowledged device command status returning through the hub. This supports the core IoT control loop without overloading the telemetry path.

findings.title: Clear split between hot queries and long-term archive
findings.explanation: Using a bounded time-series query store for recent telemetry and a separate five-year archive is a good fit for the different access patterns in the brief.

findings.title: Explicit observability on quota, latency, and command health
findings.explanation: Monitoring covers ingress throughput, processing lag, archive completeness, query latency, and command age/acknowledgement, which gives operational visibility across the main failure modes.

results.summary: A coherent Azure serverless REST API design with gateway-enforced JWT and throttling, serverless CRUD handlers, cache-aside reads, Cosmos DB persistence, and end-to-end telemetry.

findings.title: Gateway-enforced auth and throttling are well aligned
findings.explanation: The design places JWT validation, request validation, TLS termination, and per-consumer throttling at APIM, which is the right control point before serverless compute is invoked.

findings.title: Business-layer authorization is correctly repeated after the gateway
findings.explanation: The Functions layer re-checks tenant/resource authorization from verified claims before database access, preventing APIM policy checks from being the only data-isolation control.

findings.title: Cache-aside flow is coherent and mutation-safe
findings.explanation: Eligible reads can hit Redis, while successful writes invalidate affected keys after durable persistence in Cosmos DB, which supports faster repeat reads without compromising canonical state.

findings.title: Observability covers gateway, handler, cache, and database signals
findings.explanation: Application Insights receives correlated traces and metrics from APIM, Functions, Cosmos DB, and Redis, providing the latency, error, cold-start, RU, hit-rate, and memory-pressure visibility needed for this exercise.

results.summary: The design is a strong Azure identity architecture for customer registration, social federation, MFA, custom attributes, recovery, branding, and protected API access, but capacity, latency budgeting, and some compliance/ATO details need confirmation.

findings.title: Identity service covers the required customer journey breadth
findings.explanation: The chosen Azure AD B2C customer identity component directly covers registration, sign-in, social federation, MFA, password reset/recovery, branding, custom attributes, and configured risk/conditional access policies. That is a strong fit for the published core scope.

findings.title: Server-side directory management is separated from interactive sign-in
findings.explanation: The Azure Functions identity-management API and Microsoft Graph path keep privileged lifecycle operations off the customer sign-in path and use least-privilege server-side credentials, which improves isolation and reduces blast radius.

findings.title: Telemetry is privacy-filtered and scoped to operational signals
findings.explanation: Application Insights is used for journey outcomes, latency, dependency timing, and safe error categories while explicitly excluding passwords, tokens, and recovery secrets. This is a good observability choice for the stated identity scope.

findings.title: Millions-of-users capacity is not yet evidenced with sizing or limits
findings.explanation: The design selects Azure AD B2C and notes that measured capacity and tenant limits should be confirmed, but it does not show a concrete sizing approach for the published scale target of millions of users. This is a planning gap rather than a proven failure, but it still leaves the scale claim unvalidated in the submission.
findings.recommendation: Add the expected tenant sizing assumptions, quota/limit checks, and an operational scaling approach for directory operations and sign-in traffic.

findings.title: Latency target needs an explicit end-to-end strategy
findings.explanation: The gateway validates tokens and the identity service is instrumented, but the submission does not state how the full authentication journey will stay under 500ms, especially under social-federation or MFA paths that introduce extra redirects and dependency calls.
findings.recommendation: Document the latency budget per hop and the mitigation plan for redirect-heavy flows, caching, and identity-service dependency timing.

findings.title: Account-takeover prevention is implied but not described as a control path
findings.explanation: Conditional access and risk-based authentication are included, but the submission does not describe how suspicious-session detection, step-up requirements, lockout, or recovery safeguards are applied specifically to account takeover scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit ATO controls such as risk signals, step-up rules, recovery verification, and response actions for compromised accounts.

results.summary: The design is coherent for an Azure HPC cluster: Batch scheduling, H-series compute, InfiniBand MPI, HPC Cache, shared storage, and monitoring are all present. The main unresolved items are explicit queue-driven autoscaling and demonstrated 10,000+ core capacity.

findings.title: No explicit autoscaling mechanism tied to queue depth
findings.explanation: The design includes Azure Batch scheduling, a queue, and monitoring, but it does not show an autoscale rule, policy, or feedback loop that expands or shrinks the compute pool based on job queue depth. That leaves the published autoscale requirement only partially addressed.
findings.recommendation: Add the concrete autoscaling decision path, such as Batch autoscale rules or an equivalent controller that scales the H-series pool from queue length and pending runtime.

findings.title: 10,000+ core support is not demonstrated
findings.explanation: The H-series pool is described as capacity to be validated without assuming a node count, so the submission does not evidence that the cluster can reach the published 10,000+ core constraint.
findings.recommendation: State the intended pool sizing approach, SKU count, and validation plan that demonstrate the cluster can scale to 10,000+ cores.

findings.title: Core-capacity evidence is insufficient for the published scale constraint
findings.explanation: Because the design intentionally avoids assuming a node count, it does not establish compliance with the 10,000+ core constraint or show how queue-based growth reaches that scale.
findings.recommendation: Document a concrete sizing envelope for the Batch pool and show the scale-out path that gets the cluster to 10,000+ cores under load.
